# Invalid and hostile formulas

Each failure input of the spike (C-15) sits in its own fenced `math` block, so the TeX reaches the renderer exactly as written. The renderer must show the source in monospace with a subtle error mark and never crash. The three very long inputs (10,000 nested braces, 500 nested superscripts and a 5,000-term sum) are generated by the tests; this file carries a short stand-in for each.

## Malformed

lone fraction

```math
\frac{a}
```

unknown command

```math
\unknowncmd{x} + 1
```

unbalanced begin

```math
\begin{matrix} a & b
```

stray end

```math
\end{pmatrix}
```

stray brace

```math
}{
```

dangling script

```math
x^
```

open left

```math
\left( x
```

mismatched environment

```math
\begin{pmatrix} a \end{bmatrix}
```

## Macros and sizes

recursive definition

```math
\def\a{\a}\a
```

exponential macro

```math
\newcommand{\a}{\a\a}\a
```

huge rule

```math
\rule{100000em}{100000em}
```

huge space

```math
a\hspace{99999999pt}b
```

## Author controls

link

```math
\href{https://example.invalid/x}{link}
```

color

```math
\textcolor{red}{x} + \color{#00ff00} y
```

## Delimiters that are not math

An unclosed double dollar ends this sentence $$

A dollar $ with a space after it is plain text.

An unclosed $x never ends.

Four dollars $$$$ in a row are plain text.

The prices are $5 and $10 today, between $5-$10 or $5/$10, about $20,000 and $30,000 in all, and only $5. None of these is a formula.

A closing dollar before a digit does not close: $x$5 stays text.

Escaped dollars are literal even when they look like a pair: \$x\$ is three characters of text.

Code is never math: `$x$` and `$$y$$` are code spans.

```
$$ not math $$
```
